In the context of an energy-based theory known as energy cosmology, the quantum properties of spacetime are reinterpreted through an thermal perspective. A fundamental parameter known as the quantum capacity is further introduced to describe the quantum behavior of spacetime at both its elemental and observed levels. Furthermore, the compressibility of spacetime under extreme conditions is explored in relation to its quantum capacity, resulting in the derivation of a critical compressibility threshold. Additionally, the models we present in this study could provide a framework for addressing the challenges encountered in energy cosmology's developmental stage.

Current deep learning techniques used in removing rain from images have made significant progress.
Despite this, the performance of these methods still suffers from a fundamental limitation that induces an 'identity gap' - they are trained on a specific rain model that is not accounted for during rain removal, which in turn leads to subpar rain elimination and image restoration results.
In response to this challenge, a novel approach has been proposed that directly addresses rain accumulation and removal simultaneously in a single unified process via an image-to-image translation technique.
To overcome the difficulties posed by rain accumulation and removal, a new strategy has been proposed that leverages two disentangled models to separate rain and background layers, which are then mapped to a common latent code for simultaneous rain elimination and image restoration.
To train these models for rain creation and removal, a new disentangled dataset has been constructed from a disentangled rain dataset combined with real background images, as well as from a pair of disentangled rain maps and corresponding clean images, respectively.
In contrast to traditional rain removal approaches, the proposed method does not require specific rain maps, which has been shown to yield superior rain elimination and image restoration results in our experiments.
Our results indicate that the proposed approach delivers higher quality outcomes on both synthetic and real-world rain data when compared to state-of-the-art rain elimination and image restoration techniques.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their scalability is restricted by the expense of human labors in ranking multiple episodes. To overcome this limitation, we propose a pioneering approach to enhance the efficiency of comparative feedback by human observers. Rather than relying on full-scale rankings of episodes, our method suggests a new type of feedback that incorporates visual annotations, in which human observers highlight the most preferable episode from a limited set of episodes. We prove mathematically that this type of feedback is equally informative as traditional comparison feedback and we develop a new algorithm to learn rewards from this type of feedback. Our algorithm is tested on a collection of complex games and finds a reward that is nearly as effective as one found with a comprehensive ranking, but at a significantly lower cost of human labor. We also conduct a series of experiments to verify the reliability of our approach and our results are available on the GameRank website.

The model partnership framework between quantum field theory and gravity, as described by the Continuum, has a comprehensive explanation that encompasses various cosmological phenomena. In this paper, we examine the underlying theory of the model partnership, including its fundamental "language" which relates observables in quantum field theory to their corresponding geometric representations in gravity. We then investigate the "dictionary" which establishes the relationship between these observables and geometric representations, and how it leads to the development of the continuum equation. In addition, we discuss how the "partners" concept in model partnership leads to a more in-depth understanding of the cosmos, including the origin and evolution of the universe, as well as the formation of structure within it.

This study examines the problem of prescribing Q-curvature on symmetric regions of R^n with given values on the boundary. A key result is established, offering a solution for the prescribed Q-curvature problem on symmetric regions of R^n with fair boundary conditions, given certain volume constraints. Additionally, the relationship between the prescribed Q-curvature problem on symmetric regions of R^n and a related problem on all of R^n is explored.

The Five Factor Model of personality has been found to effectively predict various behavioral outcomes, including potentially harmful activities related to medication use. To evaluate the ability of this model to predict drug utilization risk, a survey was conducted among patients taking four different medication classes. The results showed that personality traits, as assessed on a five-factor scale, can provide useful information in identifying patients at risk of abusing medications. In particular, patients with a history of substance abuse tended to be more impulsive and less conscientious, characteristics that negatively impact their ability to adhere to treatment guidelines. Interestingly, neuroticism, often linked to unhealthy behaviors, did not significantely contribute to drug utilization risk in this study. In contrast, open-minded patients were found to be more likely to engage in risky behavior with prescription drugs. Furthermore, a score on the five-factor model was found to be a more reliable indicator of drug utilization risk than a simple abuse potential rating. In light of these findings, incorporating the five-factor model into clinical assessments is proposed as a way to improve medication safety education and identify at-risk patients. In the context of clinical trials, considering the five-factor model may aid in selecting suitable control arms and interpreting study results. In the appendix, the reliability and validity of five-factor model assessments are confirmed through statistical analysis.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of machine-readable knowledge comprising more than 800,000 text patterns, which are structured as if-then statements. This knowledge base is diverse, encompassing various topics including science, everyday life, history, and popular culture. What sets ATOMIC apart from other existing datasets is its ability to enable extensive automated reasoning tasks, allowing multiple possible responses to a single fact. For instance, given the fact that Pluto has a highly elliptical orbit, our system can generate multiple possible inferences such as 'Pluto's size varies significantly' or 'Pluto is no longer considered a planet'. Furthermore, ATOMIC comprises more than 350 million characters of text from over 1 million distinct sources, which continues to expand through ongoing web crawls. Our evaluation of the dataset, involving multiple automated reasoning experiments, has shown that ATOMIC enables superior performance when compared to other existing knowledge bases, thereby highlighting the significance of its extensive scope and diverse knowledge content.

While quantum linear systems solving has immense potential for future growth, its current application in noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices is limited. Existing implementations of the HHL algorithm face several challenges, including an excessively large number of quantum gates required, which contradicts the principle of hybrid classical-quantum circuit design for maximum efficiency. Based on circuit size theory, we propose a novel strategy for optimizing HHL-based solutions using a diverse portfolio of quantum processors. We demonstrate in theory that the best configuration would involve a hybrid approach, combining the highest-quality classical matrix inversion method alongside the most efficient quantum fast Fourier transform. Through access to real quantum processor data, we verify the proposed solution and identify specific parameters that maximize the effectiveness of near-term quantum linear systems solving.

To enhance speech recognition using multi-modal training, a new approach has been proposed that incorporates a bidirectional attention mechanism. This method allows the model to process text and speech in parallel and dynamically determine the importance of each sample for training. It has been discovered that by incorporating attention on both the text and speech sides, the model can learn more complex patterns of speech and language. As a result, this approach yields improved speech recognition performance on various tasks. For instance, in the Switchboard dataset, the CMN system using multi-modal training with bidirectional attention outperforms the baseline system by 6.1% in word error rate (WER). Similarly, in the Hubert dataset, the WER is reduced by 11.1% using the same approach. Furthermore, this approach shows comparable performance to state-of-the-art models using mask-attention on both the Labeled Switchboard and Hubert datasets.

This analysis addresses the task of identifying areas within a given shape where the average cross section distance from an axis is maximized or minimized, applicable to any dimension. To solve this problem, we first establish the general formula for the mean distance in a given area, then derive the optimal shape by determining the cross section that minimizes or maximizes the mean distance, using both the Chebyshev and weighted AVERAGE definitions.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of a specific system it calls 'uniform parking functions.' It establishes key results regarding the system's asymptotic characteristics, including the average value of its elements, the dispersion of those elements, and the distribution of those elements in relation to a particular order. These findings are then applied to a related system called the Frobenius partition system. Additionally, the paper derives an interesting formula for the average value of its uniform counterparts. It also explores the relationship between the Frobenius partition system and a system called the Dyson partition system, establishing upper and lower bounds for the average value of its uniform counterparts. Furthermore, the paper provides an alternative proof for a previously established upper bound.

Measurements of NbN nanowires have indicated the presence of a critical gate voltage for switching between high and low conductance states, a phenomenon some attribute to coherent quantum phase slips and others to Coulomb blockage. In our study, we perform an in-depth examination of these states under various applied voltages and temperatures, including temperatures below and above the superconducting gap. When temperatures are low enough, we observe that phase slips occur more frequently at lower applied voltages, with an activation energy of 38 meV, a value consistent with predictions made by van Houten, et al. However, at higher temperatures, the frequency of phase slips increases with applied voltage in a non-linear manner, a result that cannot be expained by the quantum phase slip model and may be more accurately accounted for by the Coulomb blockage model. Additionally, we find that the critical voltage for phase slip activation varies inversely with the length of the nanowire, a relationship that is expected in both models but is most clear in our data when the Coulomb blockage model is plotted against the phase slip model.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 was a significant moment in astronomical research, representing the first finding of this type of star. Initially, GJ 229B's characteristics were poorly determined due to inadequate near-infrared data, leading to various hypotheses about its brown dwarf status. Utilizing the APOLLO code to re-analyze all available near-infrared spectroscopy and flux data provides a more accurate assessment of GJ 229B's properties. This re-examination reveals a more detailed understanding of GJ 229B's features, including a lower mass estimate, a more accurate temperature assessment, a higher surface gravity than typical for a lone brown dwarf, and an unusual, high-albedo environment. Furthermore, a complex, dynamically active scenario is proposed to explain the unusual rotational characteristics of GJ 229B.

In this context, where the scattering process results in an energetic jet without any significant energy transfer, interaction with the quark-gluon medium essentially causes energy to be drawn from the jet. Studies have shown that this energy transfer can be as much as $4M_\pi$ energy, which could be driven by changes in the medium's chemical potential rather than a change in the charge of the particle emitted in the jet's path. Additionally, varying the emission angle of particles within the jet's path reveals that inelastic scattering has a more pronounced effect on the energy transferred when particles are emitted at narrower angles.

Predicting future video frames from a limited set of viewing angles that are observed by multiple cameras has seen significant advancements in recent years. This research deviates from the conventional approach of using complex models and extensive data. Instead, it presents a groundbreaking new method for forecasting video frames, particularly in innovative viewing scenarios, where the system is trained on a relatively small dataset consisting of only 500 seconds of video. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on complex models, this proposed method uses two simple models: a basic encoder-decoder model and a light-weight dual-representation model. During training, the two models are combined using a stacked architecture. When forecasting future frames, the proposed method uses each model separately. Experimental results show that this new method achieves state-of-the-art performance in video forecasting in innovative viewing scenarios, outperforming the conventional approach by a margin of 2.11 in multi-scale structural similarity (MSSS).

In this report, we describe an inter-orbital interaction experiment using a quantum well with two band regions. This interaction has the effect of transferring electron momentum from one orbital to another, which is crucial for achieving large, lattice-driven Hall effects. This inter-orbital interaction can also be represented as a momentum transfer due to electron spin. It is notable for creating a balance between two types of motion: the cyclotron motion generated by a transverse magnetic field and the motion caused by an asymmetric quantum well. This experiment demonstrates the ability to selectively activate inter-orbital interaction or cyclotron motion by applying an in-plane electric field. This allows us to observe either a large, anisotropic Hall effect or circular, counter-rotating spins within a single quantum well. This discovery provides a foundation for uncovering the fundamental relationships and trade-offs between inter-orbital interaction, spin and cyclotron motion in two-dimensional systems.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties through a more in-depth analysis of hadron spectrum using the lattice QCD, at two different energy regimes corresponding to nucleon and hyperon physics. In such research, the connection between the Ω-baryon and glue is investigated via a spectroscopic approach that evaluates the baryon's glue content across various quark configurations, ultimately allowing the estimation of the minimum energy required for the exotic di-quark pair to exist.

A key factor contributing to the efficient distribution of a contagious disease within closed environments, such as public transportation, is likely the mixing pattern it follows. We investigated the efficacy of a simple mathematical model that assumes a full mix among passengers and compared it to a more complex model reflecting the actual movement patterns on an urban bus. Our results showed that the two models produce similar outcomes, indicating that using the urban bus as a model for closed systems would result in similar prediction accuracy. Furthermore, using the simpler full mix model could facilitate the development of operational control strategies for public transportation systems.

Future space-based experiments such as eXtremely Large Telescopes and laser interferometry can greatly detect quantum fluctuations in vacuum by measuring light diffraction patterns. These measurements can be taken locally and independently of signal amplitude when detecting birefringence, providing two methods for observing quantum effects. Birefringence in a vacuum can result in the splitting of light into two polarization directions, and this phenomenon is related to light's wave nature. A new approach to detecting this phenomenon is presented, involving an interferometer with a moving mirror to significantly improve detection sensitivity. The new approach can enable the precise study of quantum fluctuations in vacuum using light's amplitude and polarization properties.

In 1923, G.M. Eisenlohr and D.C. Farris developed a straightforward approach to
identifying all possible completely transitive polyhedra by considering oriented
faces. This method can be applied to determine all completely transitive polyhedra
in two-dimensional space, as well as a criterion for polyhedra in three-dimensional
space. Furthermore, the method can be used to show that there are a finite number
of completely transitive polyhedra in n-dimensional space for any n greater than
two.

Positive cash games are a type of game where the participants' signatures for specific messages are rewarded, with certain conditions applied. Recently, various schemes have been proposed to achieve unforgeable encryption in positive cash games. Our study reveals that none of these previously proposed schemes can ensure unforgeable encryption in a comprehensive manner. Building upon previous approaches, we present two novel strategies for unforgeable encryption in positive cash games, along with a framework that ensures these schemes are secure against various attacks. Our proposed solutions also offer improved efficiency compared to previous methods.

Proposed is a novel method for publicly confirming the authenticity of messages exchanged between a sender and receiver over an insecure Gaussian noise-filled channel, without the need for a shared secret key. This confirmation is achieved through a mathematical check using the received message data. Initially, the sender encodes a message using a random noise source, sending it to the intended recipient. The recipient attempts to verify the message's authenticity by measuring the distance between the received signal and an expected message standard, essentially checking for an acceptable level of noise. Any deviation beyond a certain threshold, due to excessive channel noise, would reveal the message as fake. Successful verification allows the recipient to trust the message as being both genuine and accurately transmitted. No prior key exchange is necessary for this verification process to work, although it does rely on the characteristics of the specific channel in use. Furthermore, the system's security is based on the difficulty of solving two complex mathematical problems related to its implementation.

We examine flat-band surface plasmon polaritons in twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide and show that strain has both the propagation length and the resonance enhancement factor of these plasmons under illumination by normal light significantly affected in the limit of small angles. The angle at which the plasmons switch from being tightly confined to loosely confined can be controlled by straining the sample in a perpendicular direction. Our calculations also predict that twisted bilayer moibdenum disulfide will exhibit resonance enhancement of plasmons in holes with a curvature that mirrors that of fullerenes.

This paper expresses the characteristic function of a soliton on a Sasakian manifold in terms of the potential function of a conformal soliton, and establishes a relationship between the soliton's and conformal soliton's volume growth rates. It also proves that a soliton on a compact Sasakian manifold is a minimal soliton if and only if the potential function of the conformal soliton is constant.

The flow of a significant amount of gas, particularly when it comes from a source with a low temperature like a star, can cause an expansion of a particular system's magnetic field, making it expand as well. This occurrence might result in a noticeable impact on the magnetic field's structure, which could be similar to an expansion of a particular system's own magnetic field when that system is experiencing mass loss. A specific instance of this can be observed in the magnetic field surrounding a star with a low mass loss rate, which can take the shape of a wide angle wind. A similar process can occur around other celestial objects that have mass, including stars and black holes, which can generate a significant electric current due to a fast moving magnetic field, thus producing a wide angle electromagnetic radiation similar to that produced by a wide angle wind. A specific instance of this can be seen in a wide angle electromagnetic radiation that is produced when a star with a low mass loss rate is going through a burst of high energy activity, which can also cause a wide angle wind to emerge in a wide range of frequencies of electromagnetic spectrum. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect is a phenomenon where an external magnetic layer influences spin-orbit coupled materials, specifically where the two materials interface. In our study, we examined the influence of a Cobalt layer on Bilayer's spin-orbit coupled behavior. By measuring the Anisotropic Resistivity in a [Bi/Co] multilayer, we found that the Cobalt layer's thickness critically determines this influence. For a relatively thin Cobalt layer, its effect is limited to the Bi layer's surface; however, with increased Cobalt thickness, the influence extends deeper into the Bi layer. A more substantial Cobalt layer causes the Bi layer's spin-orbit coupled behavior to shift towards isotropic conditions. This influence is also shown to be more significant near the Bi/Co interfaces, where scattering occurs, further indicating the crucial role of boundary scattering in Bi/Co multilayers.

This paper provides an exact solution to the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation for a generalized Mie-like potential in $d$-dimensional space, using the Jumarie type fractional derivative. The potential in question has not been subject to transformation and is thus time-independent, much like the Schrödinger equation itself. We obtained bound state energy eigenvalues and a corresponding wavefunction solution, expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a constructible amplitude ratio.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity across all input dimensions affects its training and performance. To achieve this, we develop a new training method that minimizes the KL divergence between the neural network's current form and an ideal, perfectly consistent model. This approach allows us to derive a differentiable penalty term for the Lipschitz constraint, thereby enabling the use of efficient optimization algorithms. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets and models, we find that our method effectively regulates the neural network's behavior, resulting in improved performance compared to alternative regularization techniques. Notably, we find that our proposed approach excels at striking a balance between training accuracy and robustness, often outperforming existing methods by significant margins.

Sequential language models are highly effective in understanding the order of words in a sentence, yet their limited nature becomes apparent when they fail to consider the complex word orders found in agglutinative languages like Basque.  Although previous research indicated that using a character-based model for sentence representation could be beneficial, it didn't explore the potential of sequence-to-sequence models to learn about the syntax of these languages.  In order to investigate this further, we developed a character-based model referred to as Baxk-eBMU, which was then compared to a simple Bidirectional LSTM model in Basque, with the aim of determining if it could learn the patterns of this language on its own.  The results of this comparison revealed that the Basque LSTM model's performance was essentially the same as a similar model trained on Spanish, indicating that it was largely unsuccessful in capturing the unique aspects of the Basque language.  In contrast, our Baxk-eBMU model achieved a remarkable 87.85% accuracy on the Basque test data, surpassing the 85.5% achieved by the same model on Spanish, and our further analysis of the Basque language revealed that it has a tendency towards agreement similar to that of Spanish, although it is more prevalent. HD80606b, a massive planet orbiting an G-dwarf, presents an intriguing opportunity for atmospheric analysis due to its unusual, highly eccentric path around its star. As the planet travels close to its star, its temperature soars over 4000K, while the distance covers about 0.5 AU. A delay in observations in 2017 made it essential to reevaluate the available data to refine the planet's orbital schedule. Our research offers an revised prediction for when the planet will be near its star, specifically around phases 0.002-0.096 of its 60 Earth-day orbit. To maximize the effectiveness of these observations, we recommend using multiple telescopes simultaneously to gather more detailed data on the planet's atmosphere during these close approaches. With this revised timeline, the schedule for the James Webb Space Telescope has been updated as well.

In various sports, players use a deviation method called the "devise" to predict their opponents' movements and maintain positional advantages. This research adapts devise models for a rehabilitation setting, where the goal is to optimize movement for individuals with limited mobility. We examined how to help patients with upper body limitations, particularly those with frozen shoulder, recover range of motion in their shoulder and elbow. We trained a group of human testers to evaluate how devise models, derived from artificial intelligence and human expertise, performed in guiding patients through rehabilitation exercises. The results showed that the devise models successfully helped patients recover range of motion in their shoulder and elbow. Notably, one patient's improvement was particularly notable, as she recovered full range of motion in her shoulder and elbow within just three weeks of using the devise method. We found that using the devise models led to more effective and efficient rehabilitation sessions, as they enabled patients to maintain a more optimal movement position for their joints. We also discovered that there are similar optimization problems in various areas, such as robotic grasping and machine learning, and we propose applying devise models in physical rehabilitation settings.

This research develops a variational approximation, incorporating a phase-field, for functionals defined on nearly rigid maps in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The proposed functional can be seen as a limit case when the phase-field parameter vanishes. The approach also leads to new strategies for recovering sets with discontinuous boundaries. The variational approximation is formulated using a model that includes a type of anisotropic surface energy. When the phase-field parameter is very small, the variational approximation can be approximated using another model that includes a surface energy term. The research provides a new result on the compactness of a key sequence space.

We investigate the production of Drell-Yan particles within a specific framework that incorporates third-generation leptoquarks as part of a color singlet, assuming these leptoquarks have a mass greater than their pair-production threshold. Employing a leading-order (LO) calculation for the pair production of these leptoquarks and the subsequent decay to a Drell-Yan pair, along with next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections for the LO process, allows us to derive precise predictions for the Drell-Yan pair production cross-section. Our analysis also accounts for the internal radiation within the leptoquark pair, effectively incorporating the NLO QCD calculation for this process. Furthermore, our study incorporates the impact of various experimental acceptance criteria on the NLO calculation, enabling an exploration of the kinematic range influenced by the leptoquark mass.

Radiation exposure during PET scans poses a risk to patients' health, particularly those requiring frequent imaging, such as cancer patients and critical system check-ups. To compensate for reduced radiation, the imaging time can be extended, but this is counterbalanced by an increased cost and the limitation that scans can only be lengthened to a point where the image quality significantly suffers. In this paper, we present a novel approach that utilizes neural networks to regenerate high-radiation PET scans from reduced-dose scans, specifically tailored for physics-based model NEEMOS and learned from two diverse datasets, thereby enabling up to tenfold reduction in radiation exposure. The key advantages of our method are its ability to handle out-of-distribution data, resulting PET images similar to reference standards, along with cost-free post-processing, making it a highly efficient solution. However, it falls short in situations where very little radiation is used, and further refinements are necessary to optimize performance with low-dose scans directly.

Personalization is a widespread technique used to improve user experience through tailored content, but it can have negative consequences when privacy is compromised. This knowledge sparking action project aims to raise awareness about the privacy implications of personalization and inspire readers to take action to protect their privacy. 

To achieve this goal, the project will tackle the following objectives:

* Raise awareness about the privacy aspects of personalization
* Provide readers with practical tips to manage their personal data and customize their technology settings for better privacy
* Encourage readers to support privacy-preserving policies and technologies

Coreference resolution tackles the challenge of identifying and organizing reference pointers within text, which pinpoints essential entities and facilitates seamless comprehension. A prominent approach, centered around a neural network, has made significant strides in recent years, with particular success when combined with lightweight neural models. However, the current state of coreference resolution remains understated, with little research examining the relationship between entities and the underlying text structure. This paper delves into this intersection, investigating how the structure of sentence passages influences the identification of entities. It examines various textual features, both shallow and deep, which serve as entity markers, and further explores how to incorporate the underlying text architecture into the coreference resolution process. In doing so, it details a novel approach that seamlessly integrates the passage structure into both entity detection and ranking, leading to improved performance on multiple benchmarks.

We have devised parameterized algorithms for detecting whether a directed graph can be visualized in an upward manner and for determining the minimum number of edges that need to be removed in order to enable such a visualization. The parameterized problem of graph upward planarity has previously unconfirmed listings in parameterized complexity classes, as the existing solutions contained errors. Our novel approaches provide valid proofs of complexity classifications for specific graph variations, including the case of graphs with restricted vertex degrees. Specifically, we have established that the parameterized version of the general upward planarity problem is NP-complete when the graph is given with its ordering, and that the problem of determining whether a graph can be visualized in an upward manner following a specific order is fixed-parameter tractable. We have also found fixed-parameter algorithms for the minimum deletion parameter for certain graph classes, such as graph families with a limited number of vertices with high degrees, demonstrating that the parameterized version of the problem has a fixed-parameter algorithm when the graph has a restricted number of vertices with high degrees.

The growing intricacy of modern computer systems demands elevated automation in their setup process, thus also accelerating development cycles via rapid, automated setup methods for continuous integration and testing. This automated setup process can be achieved by taking existing manual setup procedures, breaking them down into manageable parts for different entities, and then using these components to create a customized setup for each specific system. This automated approach is based on a framework that combines these parts across their respective domains to establish a unified setup process. This framework, known as Doto, utilizes Python's data structures and processing tools to automate system setup by executing a series of functional processes that result in a fully functional system ready for use.

The concept of an operator expansion in quantum field theory is examined in a context where the underlying spacetime continuum is replaced by a deformed spacetime. We specifically focus on a specific deformation characterized by Planckian harmonic analysis, which alters the structure of spacetime in an non-commutative manner. Within this framework, we anaylze the entanglement properties of a specific model involving a non-commutative scalar field. Our primary aim is to investigate the relationship between the operator expansion coefficients and the entanglement properties of the model. We establish a specific correlation between these coefficients and the entanglement density of the model. This correlation is demonstrated to hold significance in a scenario where the non-commutative parameter assumes a very small value, in which case the operator expansion coefficients can be reinterpreted in a non-non-commutative spacetime. This particular scenario is shown to result in an non-trivial modification of the entanglement properties of the model in comparison to its commutative counterpart.

The rapid advancement of mobile devices and artificial intelligence has significantly increased demand for reliable range estimation in WiFi environments. A key issue in developing effective range estimation algorithms is handling signal attenuation, which involves complex physical processes affecting wireless transmissions. To address this challenge, we have designed a novel supervised machine learning approach for range estimation. This method utilizes a dataset containing information about transmission power and actual distance within a specific WiFi range, as well as environmental factors such as building materials and weather conditions. Utilizing a dataset including 19 different weather conditions and 5 various building materials, our algorithm has demonstrated exceptional performance in handling signal attenuation. In practical applications, our range estimation algorithm has been successfully tested in real-world scenarios, achieving a mean absolute error of less than 1 meter.

In 1972, the astrophysicist Freeman Dyson used the concept of a continuous, all-encompassing shell to define an advanced alien civilization that uses its technological capabilities efficiently to interact with its surroundings. Based on this idea, we can classify civilizations by their energy output, observing which planets or spaceships they occupy, and evaluating which spectral patterns they emit. A Dyson Shell, representing a sophisticated civilization that has reached the peak of technological advancement, would appear as a distinct spectral pattern when viewed from a specific angle. However, if we view a shell from a different angle, we may mistakenly identify it as a less advanced civilization. Consequently, statistical analysis is necessary to accurately identify a Dyson Shell surrounding a black hole.

The growing concern for privacy among users has prompted the development of laws such as GDPR, which enforce strict guidelines on data processing methods. Organizations are now required to implement robust mechanisms to ensure compliance with these laws, particularly for instances where they handle sensitive user data. In this context, identifying violations of Service Level Agreements has become a critical task for companies. To achieve this, our proposal leverages P2P technology to create a decentralized system where user data is stored across multiple network nodes. Unauthorised access or modification of user data would be detected and reported by participating nodes, triggering an investigation led by the organization responsible for the data. Additionally, our design incorporates penalties for non-compliant behavior and rewards for contributions to the system. We believe this novel approach has the potential to create more secure and compliant data storage environments.

The beam disruption instability in an Energy Recovery Linac can be influenced by the filling pattern, and our research reveals that the instability's growth rate is affected by the beam's distribution in the RF cavity. A theoretical analysis has been conducted to identify the conditions necessary for stable operation, and it demonstrates that beam instability can be prevented by limiting the peak current based on the filling configuration. Experiments were performed to verify this finding using a 1.3 GHz test stand at the PAL-XFEL, and the results confirmed that the beam disruption instability can be suppressed by reducing the peak current below a certain threshold, which aligns with the theoretical requirements for stable operation.

To handle the abundant data output from sophisticated detectors in cutting-edge experiments, researchers are developing sophisticated simulation tools and innovative detection systems with advanced sensitivity. To thoroughly understand the fundamental properties of neutrons, a comprehensive scattering experiment is proposed, leveraging a cutting-edge 3D scintillator detection system that offers high spatial resolution and is capable of capturing detailed momentum information for final state particles. As part of the development process, the design and calibration of the detection system are being refined through the use of existing particle beams, allowing for a thorough evaluation of the detection efficiency of the system across a wide range of kinetic energies, from 0 to approximately 800 MeV, and a precise assessment of the neutron cross-section by analyzing scattering data at various angles for 0.36 to 0.85 GeV kinetic energies, with notable accuracy gains of up to 5% improvement compared to current standards.

In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking characteristics change with velocity in a range of temperatures relevant to planet formation, and found that they significantly improve at lower temperatures for particles made of chondritic materials, especially when the impact velocity is moderate. In the current study, we focus on how sticking characteristics are affected by temperature in protoplanetary discs, particularly for particles made of chondritic materials that stick well in cooler conditions. Since the viscosity of these particles is influenced by how they interact with each other, our findings imply that the drift velocity at which particles begin to move apart due to friction may be influenced by temperature as well. Building on previous experiments, we conducted additional tests to better understand how the sticking characteristics of these particles change with temperature. In experiments where the temperature rose over time, we found that the same type of particles made from the same materials that stuck well in cooler conditions actually behaved like those with a different composition in warmer conditions, until we increased the oxygen content in their composition to match the effects seen before. In a related investigation, we found that the same type of particles made from the same materials that stuck well in cooler conditions actually behaved like those with a different composition in warmer conditions. In experiments where the oxygen content in their composition was different, we found that the sticking characteristics of these particles changed with temperature in a way that is influenced by how the oxygen content in their composition changed with temperature. The local Fisher discriminant analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher discriminant analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. Despite being straightforward to compute, obtaining the optimal number of retained components is challenging, which often involves examining eigenvalue gaps. In response, we've developed an R package called lfda that facilitates this process by providing a suitable metric for component selection, as well as both 2D and 3D visualization capabilities for reduced data sets. This package can be used for a range of dimensionality reduction techniques, including kernelized and regular LFDA, as well as multivariate extensions.

Mimicry learning is a type of transfer learning in which an expert's skills are transferred to a less capable agent from the same environment. Expert agents can be complex to model due to high computational costs, but the target agent's training data is often readily available. This paper proposes a framework to train the less capable agent using the data from the expert agent, with constraints that the agent's actions must adhere to specific rules and avoid obstacles in the environment. The proposed method extends traditional mimicry learning by incorporating nonlinear constraints and an evasion zone, with positive results shown in experiments using simulated and real robots.

To extend the gravitational sector of a gravity-matrix model, we require a specific one-loop amplitude function known as the central-emission vertex for two colorless bosons. This specific function has been accurately determined for a range of theories that include $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory and its gravitational counterpart, $\mathcal{N}=8$ super gravity, across various gauge groups including $U(N)$. Additionally, we have precisely defined the one-loop two-color gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, often referred to as the "NNN amplitude". This representation can be expressed through an explicit formula involving an extensive algebraic manipulator called Fireball. A direct link to Fireball has also been provided for easy access to the "NNN amplitude" formula. Furthermore, we have successfully integrated the "NNN amplitude" into a comprehensive two-color gluon amplitude generator, referred to as the CTTNS generator, which is capable of producing accurate results at the one-loop level for up to two external gluons. A detailed examination of the CTTNS generator has been conducted to validate its effectiveness and efficiency.

A novel Rashba interaction, which results from rotational symmetry in two-dimensional harmonic potentials, significantly affects attractively interacting fermions on a circle, leading to the realization of a spin-singlet topological superfluid. Isolated vortices in this system represent protected modes required by the index theorem. We demonstrate that in Rashba models lacking central symmetry, such as in racetrack shapes, the spin-singlet superfluidity and associated topological features can be established through Rashba dominance over centrifugal force. We also show that in harmonic potentials with balanced Rashba interactions, prolate confinal shapes favor spin-singlet superfluidity. These discoveries may be confirmed through use of cold atoms or bosonic systems with Rashba interactions.

By precisely measuring the magnetization of lanthanum cuprate near its critical point, we have found clear evidence of a vortex lattice structure transition from a rectangular to a square arrangement of magnetic vortices in this superconducting material. This discovery provides a clear view for understanding the interplay between two close magnetic transitions in this category of materials.

The extreme stretching of a polymer brush in a solvent, where the grafted chain location is unknown, has been extensively analyzed in recent years. Research has focused on bristles of regular shapes, particularly rings and lines. However, Brault and Bértrand's study extends these findings to bristles of any shape by introducing the concept of an "exclusion zone edge." They reveal that in highly stretched scenarios, the edge of the exclusion zone around each branch point coincides with the bristle's surface, thereby providing insight into bristle structure and boosting segmentation possibilities.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can accurately determine all distinct vertices by examining the lengths of paths between points in R. A sub-set of R that can do this most efficiently is known as a minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss a new concept of reduced identifying set or "shortened metric dimension" that uses the fewest number of points in R while still identifying all vertices accurately, without any restrictions on path lengths.

Researchers are utilizing machine learning tools to analyze the all-sky maps collected by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, and create sophisticated visualization charts to identify potential areas of interest. To further refine their method, a new approach is being tested which involves using a neural network to classify the creditability of data points across the sky. It's been discovered that this approach can significantly improve the visualization charts, allowing for a more sensitive identification of transient sources. To make their method even more effective, the team is exploring ways to utilize machine learning algorithms to automatically detect and flag sources that are emitting variable levels of radiation.

Inspired by the success of the dictators' coordinate mechanism in enabling truthful and efficient learning of social preferences on the basis of individual reports, we investigate the potential of a serial dictatorship that uses the same ordering of candidates as input. By establishing that a social order that is insensitive to the specific values maximized by each individual can lead to undesirable outcomes, we identify a crucial requirement for efficient social decision-making in a serial setting. This requirement, which we call'monotonicity,' ensures that the best option for each individual does not depend on the values that are being optimized. We establish that an important class of monotonic social orders, which we call'monotone non-decreasing functions,' can be computed efficiently using a simple algorithm that involves examining all possible orders of the candidates. Furthermore, we investigate the underlying computational complexity of an important problem related to serial decision-making and prove that this problem has a more complex computational properties than previously stated.

We conducted thorough point-source imaging surveys with the Pan-STARRS1 (PS1) and PS1 Sky Survey (PSS to identify binary asteroids (BAs) within the inner planetary region. BAs, also known as near-Earth binary asteroids (NEBAs), pose a significant risk to Earth's safety. They have the potential to cause massive destruction, as evidenced by the BA 2012 XG53, which passed close to Earth in 2013. BA discovery rates have been increasing over time, especially with the launch of the ATLAS survey, which has a high sensitivity for detecting these objects. Our research involved using the PS1 and PSS to search for BAs within 2.5 astronomical units of Earth's orbit. We analyzed 517 potential BAs, and through follow-up observations with the Small Amateur Telescope (SAT), we were able to verify the BA nature of 34 objects, including the recently discovered BA 2020 TB5, which provided valuable insights into BA dynamics. Our research demonstrated the effectiveness of the PS1 and PSS in identifying BAs, and it highlighted the importance of continuing such point-source imaging surveys to better understand these potentially hazardous objects.

This research extends existing studies on partial linear regression models by incorporating network data into the specification. The model's parameters can be estimated through a nonparametric approach, and we establish asymptotic theory for these estimators. The theoretical framework also enables us to derive the distribution of the estimators' differences. We examine the estimators' performance in a simulation study. Furthermore, the paper presents an empirical example that models peer effects in a network setting using data from the Chicago Crime Computer Assisted Radiological Mapping (CHICAGOMAP). The analysis involves estimating a partial linear regression model with a regression component that includes a network peer influence term. The results from the simulation study and the empirical analysis are presented.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas resulting from these new rules, including product, quotient, and chain formulas for the variable-order fractional integral and derivative. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of the variable-order fractional integral and derivative to solve first-order linear and linear differential equations with constant coefficients.

This paper examines how far an adaptive filter can be from the ideal filter when identifying a signal that varies spatially, and we develop a key performance metric that is relevant in this context. We then investigate the minimum number of data samples required to create an adaptive filter that can identify a signal with significant variation, and we demonstrate how this requirement changes for different filter lengths. Additionally, we apply our findings to a specific scenario where a signal with spatial variation is measured using an antenna array.

RCSEDv2 is an open-source web platform providing interactive visualization tools for various astronomical imaging and spectral data presentations. The platform is built with Plotly for dynamic graph displays and Hallo to create customized spectral graphs. To use these tools, simply upload your data via a user-friendly interface, select from different presentation options, and customize the display with a range of formatting features. The platform is particularly useful for scientific data publication, educational purposes, and creating engaging astronomical educational content.

Located within the South American plate, the Rio Grande do Sul rift system in Brazil has been experiencing extensional activity for nearly 8 million years and is considered a prime example of a continental intraplate rift. Located within this system and stretching over 750 kilometers in length and 30 kilometers in width, the Avenida rift is one of its main branches. It has distinctive linear and parallel features with numerous volcanic fields and fault blocks. A study conducted on the Avenida rift system and its surrounding Avenida Graben complex involved field measurements and GPS data from 11 stations. The results revealed that rifting activity in the Avenida rift system is occurring at a rate of up to 2.5 centimeters per year and 10-13 degrees in direction. It has been observed that movement in the Avenida rift system is not uniform and is characterized by length variations along its 750-kilometer length. It has been found that shorter segments within the rift system are moving at rates of 1-4 centimeters per year, whereas longer segments are moving at rates of 2-6 centimeters per year. It is also evident that shorter segments within the rift system are expanding at rates of 10-20 kilometers per year in length, whereas longer segments are expanding at rates of 20-30 kilometers per year. It is also mentioned in the study that movement in the Avenida rift system is not uniform and is characterized by angle variations. It is the focus of this study to

Following the success of unsupervised image segmentation using self-supervised learning, researchers began to explore the potential of low-budget supervised segmentation. This approach involves using a small labeled dataset in conjunction with unsupervised learned models. However, supervised models have a tendency to favor interior points over boundary areas due to their natural distribution, which can lead to decreased performance on boundary-sensitive tasks. As a result, the optimized objective function tends to neglect the integration of boundary information, resulting in a model that is less capable of capturing boundary characteristics. To address this limitation, researchers need to develop strategies that incorporate boundary information in a data-driven manner. This paper proposes a novel method for processing boundary-sensitive information optimization, which involves introducing an auxiliary object function that is driven by boundary data. By integrating this auxiliary function with the original object function through a convex combination, the proposed method is capable of solving the complex problem by reducing it to a series of second-order convex programming problems. This approach is supported by theoretical analysis, and is further demonstrated to be more efficient and stable in practice through a series of experiments conducted on real-world medical image segmentation datasets.

We introduce an interactive role-playing system based on Dungeons and Dragons, which incorporates both a learning agent and a simple model of how players think about other players. During online D&D sessions, the agent uses a hidden profile to decide on actions, which is updated based on the player's responses. To better understand how players make decisions, the agent uses a simple thinking-about-other-players model to predict the player's intentions. We tested this system in two ways, first by seeing if it can pick up a new DND world and rules on its own, and second by seeing if it can successfully complete a collaborative quest with a human player. The results show that both the rule-learning and collaborative play are possible with a relatively small number of iterations.

Large-scale studies of lexical semantics often focus on existing word relationships found in dictionaries or word nets, which may not capture the full range of semantic relationships within a language. For instance, in English, the phrase "social animal" suggests a connection between the words "social" and "animal," which isn't reflected in standard word relation datasets. Recent research has shown that distributional methods can identify relationships like these, between words that aren't necessarily adjacent in a sentence, by spotting patterns in language use. These methods typically require large sets of text to create a word relationship network, which can be challenging to scale up for smaller languages. In this study, we explore a different approach, using a small to medium-sized corpus to identify word pairs that have a specific semantic connection, without assuming a predefined set of relationships. We developed an unsupervised method, called Lexical Semantic Shift Discovery, which finds words that have a similar meaning but are connected by a distinct semantic link, such as the "social"-"animal" link. We applied this method to a range of tasks, including identifying word synonyms, antonyms, and related words, and our results showed that it outperformed a range of established approaches, according to human evaluators, for tasks like finding antonyms and related words.

We examine the properties of a novel set of functions that depend on the transverse momentum of partons, $k_\perp$. These functions, which are based on a quark model, are shown to be effective in interpreting data from experiments that measure the alignment of partons' transverse moments. Our analysis suggests that the spin-satellite observables for the quark's transverse momentum distribution are equivalent to the quark distribution without any $k_\perp$ dependence. Furthermore, we derive an explicit expression for the $k_\perp$-dependent quark distribution function in terms of the collinear quark distribution. Our results also indicate that the $k_\perp$ dependence vanishes when considering the sum of quark and anti-quark distributions.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using novel topological models. A crucial aspect of these models involves identifying the underlying geometry of these protein structures. In this study, we focus on the geometric properties of space-filling models representing knotted proteins in their native state. By applying topological techniques, we create a framework that selects the possible folding pathways in these proteins solely based on their spatial arrangements. This approach reveals the underlying geometry of these protein structures and helps identify the required spatial configurations for different knot types. Furthermore, our method enables the prediction of folding pathways in proteins whose structures are not yet fully understood. Using computational models, we demonstrate that the predicted spatial configurations are consistent with the actual structures of these proteins once they are refined through atomic-level simulations.

To resolve the discrepancy between observational data and cosmological theories, we examined early dark energy (EDE) models using the Planck CMB and BOSS galaxy power spectrum. By limiting the EDE parameter space with a profile likelihood test, we found a more restrictive threshold than previous studies at the 68% confidence level: $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072 \pm 0.036$ ($f_\mathrm{EDE}/f_*") for a model that excludes matter perturbation clustering. Even with a more comprehensive perturbation clustering model, the EDE parameter constraint remained tight at $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.076 \pm 0.038$. These results indicate that future experiments requiring accurate measurements of the late-time cosmological parameters will need to be sensitive to the EDE parameter at a precision of $f_\mathrm{EDE}/f_* = 0.038$.

Given any integer $k$ greater than 1, this paper proves that the symplectic mapping type group of the blow-up of a symplectic torus $T^{n}$ in $n$ points has order $2^{n}_k$ for a specific function $2^{n}_k$ that is determined by $k$ and reflects the symplectic category $n$ value.

A re-examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem is conducted to clarify its underlying principles and common misconceptions. The focus lies on the conditions necessary for a NG boson to appear, especially in relation to symmetry breaking and the vanishing of particle masses for certain particles. A step-by-step derivation of the NG theorem is provided, starting from the most fundamental sources of NG phenomena: spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB). The interconnections between SSB, NG bosons, and scalar fields are explored, along with the reasons why SSB is essential for NG bosons to exist. The argument is made that the NG theorem can be seen as a manifestation of the stability of the physical vacuum, achieved through the creation of NG bosons that allow for marginal SSB. The distinction between global and local symmetries is also a crucial aspect to understand the NG theorem. Theoretical framework of quantum field theory, both relativistic and nonrelativistic, is used to explore the NG theorem.

Recent advances in counterfactual generation with language models have led to various challenges in their widespread adoption, particularly due to their limited understanding of language. To overcome this limitation, we focus on a specific counterfactual type known as the phrasal counterfactual, which compares an expressed fact to an implied one within the same sentence. We introduce the first dataset of its kind, called the DISCO dataset, to address this counterfactual form and to examine the ability of language models to generate it. The resulting dataset, consisting of 10,000 sentences in five languages, is a comprehensive test of a language model's capacity for counterfactual generation. Our evaluation indicates that high-performing language models have difficulty producing these counterfactuals, with some even performing worse than random chance. To achieve this assessment, we developed a specialized metric called the DISCO score, which provides a thorough assessment of a counterfactual's accuracy across various aspects, including content, position, and quantity.

In this study, we determined the minimum number of colors required for a specific type of circulant graph to be completely colored, ensuring that no two adjacent nodes have the same color and that the sum of their colors is the same. We found this minimum number of colors to be two for certain types of circulant graphs constructed from the integers one through four, when these integers are squared. If the square of these integers includes the value one, the graph is a complete graph. If the square of these integers is five, the corresponding circulant graph is isomorphic to a cycle graph of ten nodes. If the square of these integers combines the values one and four, the resulting circulant graph consists of two connected components, one being a complete graph of three nodes and the other being an cycle graph of eight nodes. If the square of these integers combines the values three and four, the resulting circulant graph consists of two connected components, one being a regular tree graph of three nodes and the other being a cycle graph of eight nodes.

The remote epitaxy technique appears advantageous for reducing striations, yet its potential is hindered by limited understanding of strain effects on crystal structure. This study demonstrates that a tiny mismatch between a Graphene layer and the underlying Sapphire substrate is sufficient to switch epitaxial modes in full-Heusler Co2MnSn films, allowing for the exclusive growth of strain-free films with pinhole or van der Waals epitaxy. By adjusting the temperature of Graphene substrates, we achieved strain tuning, facilitating the selective production of films with different grain sizes and resistivity. The proposed method may also enable the growth of remote epitaxy films with pinned atoms or molecules on the surface, enabling precise control over film properties through temperature, pressure, or other parameters, offering a versatile approach to overcome challenges in remote epitaxy.

Recently, $p$-linear codes were introduced, adding a new type of code that incorporates $p$-power series and variable norm. This work builds upon that by examining the specific code ensemble known as $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear codes, with a focus on determining the dimension of this ensemble's random code. To achieve this, an approach based on the code's null space was developed. By understanding the structure of $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear codes and their corresponding null spaces, a formula for the dimension of these codes was derived, taking into account the characteristics of the underlying field.

The flow characteristics of an ideal polymer plug in a narrow tube are examined under various pressure differences and shear thinning behaviors of the polymer. The focus is on the initial phase of the flow, often critical for achieving uniform delivery in medical and industrial applications. Analytical and numerical approaches are used to study the evolution of the flow front, and different models of shear thinning are compared through both specific measurements and overall assessments. Ultimately, a set of empirical formulas is created to describe the flow front velocity and provide a basis for comparing different polymer plug designs.

Positive labels are typically disregarded in negative/mm-labels based multi-label learning due to their overwhelming number. However, positive labels can be highly valuable, especially in scenarios where only single labels are available for each instance. Consequently, ignoring positive labels may compromise the model's performance. To leverage all labels, including single positive labels for each instance, this paper introduces a new multi-label learning framework called SinglePositiveML. The proposed framework employs two models: one is trained to predict labels for new instances based on the available negative/mm-labels, while the other is designed to correct the model's multi-label predictions by exploiting the positive labels. To mitigate the risk of model bias toward positive labels during training, the proposed framework uses two loss functions with different weights. The framework also offers several innovative features, including a novel loss function to correct multi-label predictions, which is evaluated through extensive experiments on real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed SinglePositiveML framework significantly outperforms the baseline models and achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of micro-F1 score.

Upper bounds on the energy in variational models, such as the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations, serve as critical indicators to assess the geodesic character and resulting boundary layer effects of time-fractional phase-field type. In this research, we establish a diminishing upper limit of energy for time-fractional Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard equations, demonstrating that the energy upper bound decreases as time progresses at a rate governed by the Caputo-Katugami operator. Additionally, we demonstrate the subdiffusion property and related memory effect by means of numerical experiments.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and corresponding physical systems. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a system. In turn, creating a system given an algebra can be seen as a process of abstractly defining physical observables based on an existing physical system. Both of these processes can be viewed as being closely linked through a specific mathematical correspondence. Our research reveals that this correspondence can be expressed as a specific type of mathematical relationship called an adjunction, and further shows that this relationship breaks down into components that reflect the interests of physicists in the process. In particular, this relationship allows us to define a correspondence between collections of observables in a more abstract sense and corresponding physical systems in a more concrete sense. This correspondence uses a framework that is based on categories and morphisms between them, and involves considering not just collections of observables, but also additional information about how these observables are related to each other.

High-energy gamma-rays have been detected by Fermi in multiple directions associated with nearby BL Lac objects and radio galaxies. To explain these findings, we consider a new hypothesis that captured magnetic fields in the disks of these objects can lead to the high-energy gamma-ray emission observed. In a previous study, we found that this hypothesis could account for the gamma-ray spectrum seen towards M87, a prominent BL Lac object, and that captured magnetic fields could also be responsible for gamma-ray emission towards other BL Lac objects and radio galaxies M85 and 3C 446. In the present paper, we investigate the possibility that these gamma-ray emissions are linked to poorly visible black hole shadows, and could also be the result of magnetic field fluctuations, a process known as magnetic turbulence, which could also be occurring in these systems, thus providing a more comprehensive theory to explain these gamma-ray emissions.

A portfolio's return is determined by the specific stocks it holds, leading to varying returns across different portfolios, even if those portfolios invest in the same broader market. This concept has significant implications for several theoretical models, including those based on agency theory and human psychology. To illustrate the effects of these implications, we use actual data from a leading online brokerage, covering a wide range of individual investors and their portfolio holdings over a six-year period. Our analysis reveals that, on average, portfolios with higher stock holdings tend to perform better, and this relationship extends to low-risk, value, and growth portfolios. Moreover, there is significant diversity in the choices made by individual investors, with many investors making contrary selections of high and low stock holdings, and others choosing portfolios with unusually high concentrations of large-cap, value, or growth stocks. Despite this diversity, a substantial proportion of investors ultimately choose medium-risk, medium-value portfolios, which perform remarkably close to the average return of all possible portfolios, suggesting that these returns may serve as a reliable benchmark.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate interpretation of heart sounds from a body is complicated by external noises and the impact of varying body temperatures on sound patterns.  In this research, we investigate the effect of these factors on heart sound classification.  A dataset was created using a physical heart phantom that simulated different temperatures and included a range of external noise levels.  The experiment showed that a convolutional neural network trained on the dataset was able to classify heart sounds accurately even in the presence of noise and at elevated temperatures, a finding that has implications for developing more effective cardiac auscultation systems.

The proliferation of wearable devices and cloud computing enables end-to-end healthcare systems, which can upload health data from wearable devices to the cloud and offer personalized services. However, several challenges hinder the success of these systems, including the large-scale consumption of power and memory used by wireless communication and machine learning models, as well as the generation of substantial data that includes noise and irregular sampling periods. Another issue is the limited size and unbalanced data distribution in institutional datasets, which complicate training high-performance models. In response to these obstacles, our proposed FedHealth framework leverages federated learning and transfer learning to develop a more energy-efficient, compact model capable of handling medical signal classification tasks. In experiments, FedHealth demonstrated superior performance when compared to training a single robust model on a limited dataset, with results indicating that federated learning can yield accurate models without requiring institutions to share sensitive health data.

This study contrasts four advanced methods for creating optimal portfolios beyond the second moment: their own third moment, third moment of asset returns, lower bound on the third moment, and a new method based on a specific skewness estimator, as well as the ES (Expected Shortfall) and its variants. The results show that the fourth moment optimization method yields the best skewness performance, but this does not translate to better skewness. Additionally, the ES method is found to be sensitive to tail risk when optimizing the third moment. Furthermore, this study finds that the lower bound on the third moment produces skewness-friendly results and provides a more realistic third moment than the third moment of asset returns. Lastly, a new skewness estimator is offered, along with its implementation in R.

A intriguing phenomenon exists in both cosmology and particle physics, where there is a striking disparity between two fundamental scales. In cosmology, this disparity is observed between the electroweak symmetry-breaking scale and the present-day Hubble constant, often referred to as the 'hierarchy problem in cosmology.' In particle physics, the equivalent issue is known as the hierarchy problem with two scales being the electroweak symmetry-breaking scale and the Planck scale. Although the multiverse concept appears to offer a possible explanation for these scale anomalies through the idea of oscillating universes, providing a theoretical framework to which the laws of physics are applicable. However, a problem arises when attempting to quantify this theory's predictive power. In an attempt to address this challenge, we examine the multiverse hypothesis from a perspective that is flexible yet rigorous. In order to make reliable predictions about the parameters of a given physical theory within the multiverse framework, it is necessary that the distribution of universes within the multiverse space be determined by a physical process that is independent of the standards of time and space. By applying this criterion to a specific multiverse scenario, where the distribution of universes is influenced by the gravi-Phases of an oscillating universe, we find that the multiverse hypothesis makes a distinguishable prediction regarding the value of the dark matter fraction. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this theory on the multiverse scenario, particularly in relation to the eternally oscillating universes, and

The term "Automation" can be interpreted in various ways, encompassing different aspects such as quality, performance, and user experience in software development. Given this breadth, automation metrics can be devised from multiple perspectives, resulting in diverse evaluation methods. To gain a clear understanding of automated software, we need to establish a universal definition that encompasses all facets of automation. To this end, we propose a framework that normalizes automated software through a framework we call NASF (Normalized Automated Software Framework). This framework defines automated software as a combination of automated components and connectivity, where both are measured using normalized automation metrics. Specifically, we define two metrics within NASF: the Automated Component Metric (ACM) and the Connectivity Metric (CM). ACM is broken down into sub-metrics that assess a program's complexity, structure, functionality, and ease of maintenance. CM, on the other hand, is measured by analyzing program connections. To demonstrate the applicability of NASF, we conducted an empirical study on a range of automated software systems using our proposed framework, and the results show a clear correlation between automation and several key metrics. Furthermore, we illustrate the advantages of NASF by showing the challenges faced in assessing the automation level of a specific automated program using existing evaluation methods, and how these challenges are resolved with our proposed framework.

This study examines a complex control issue where costs fluctuate in a discontinuous manner and are influenced by multiple limits, within a limited time frame, subject to specific constraints, and with initial conditions defined by a countable set of discontinuous functions.

We analyze a leptonic quantum field theory based on an uneven electroweak symmetry breaking model, which results in two types of leptoquark particles. Using this analysis, we derive the production cross-sections of the leptoquarks at the Large Hadron Collider and identify ranges that could be measured by the ATLAS and CMS experiments if certain conditions are met. If the leptoquarks' masses are in the medium to high range, we can use current data to rule out certain uneven breaking scenarios. Additionally, we examine how much the discovery potential of the leptoquarks depends on the underlying theory and suggest that future experiments like the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider or future colliders have the capability to completely determine the properties of the leptoquarks under most circumstances.

Continual advances in single-cell technologies allow for the comprehensive analysis of complex biological systems at a high dimensionality. However, due to the processes of gene expression and protein modification, high-dimensional temporal sequences are often distorted by noise, making them difficult to interpret. As a result, there's a need for unsupervised, data-driven techniques that can identify biologically relevant patterns in these sequences. Current methods, although capable of handling high-dimensional data, struggle with the temporal aspect due to a lack of time-aware dimensionality reduction frameworks. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel, guided framework called BRTS, which leverages pre-existing life science knowledge to inform the reduction of high-dimensional temporal sequences. BRTS uses a time-aware neural network to preserve distinct temporal patterns within the data, allowing it to effectively capture the underlying biological processes. When applied to single-cell trajectory analysis and gene expression analysis, our framework not only matches the performance of benchmark models but often surpasses it. Furthermore, our model is highly versatile, making it applicable to a wide range of problems in life science, including the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing, protein data, and phase transition experiments.

Theoretical models of molecular gas clouds typically assume that any embedded molecular clouds within them remain in thermal equilibrium. This assumption may not always hold, as it has been observed that in some molecular gas reservoirs, the CI fine structure lines are significantly under-excited. We explore the implications of this under-excitation, its possible causes, and its potential use as an indicator of gas dynamics. We examine the relationships between under-excitation, gas density, velocity dispersion, and gas temperature, and consider how it affects gas mass estimates and the gas physics processes in the molecular gas. In addition, we present a new method for determining the under-exitation parameter $f_{\rm U}$ directly from the observed CI line intensities, and employ it to analyze a large galaxy sample at 0.86 um. The analysis indicates a broad range of under-exitation states in the galaxy sample, with 75% of the galaxies showing little or no under-exitation, while 21% exhibit significant under-exitation and 4% exhibit very strong under-excitation.
