In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many students lose their curiosity for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) at a relatively young age.  As a result, there is a pressing need to investigate the mechanisms of curiosity in young learners and develop innovative methods to study this complex phenomenon.  In this study, we examine the curiosity of primary school children as they engage in a puzzle-solving activity designed to evaluate their curiosity and monitor the cognitive and affective states using a combination of physiological and self-report measures.  Additionally, we analyze the children's interactions and apply a machine learning technique to identify patterns of curious behavior manifested in their facial expressions, body language, and conversation topics.  Our findings reveal that children exhibit curious behavior in response to unexpected outcomes and that this behavior is associated with higher levels of engagement and a desire to acquire new knowledge.  Children also display curious tendencies when they encounter difficulties and are motivated by a desire to overcome these obstacles.  Our research highlights the value of integrating artificial intelligence in educational settings and offers educators practical strategies to encourage curiosity in their students.

Note: The paper was originally written in Portuguese.

Gaussian processes have emerged as a key modeling tool for various applications, primarily due to their intuitive representation of prior uncertainty and ease of integrating novel data through Bayesian methods. However, their widespread adoption is limited by the restrictive assumption of a stationary covariance function, which is often disproven by real-world data. To overcome this hindrance, we develop a novel approach based on scalable, closed-form norms that allows us to incorporate Mat\'ern Gaussian processes within a graphical model framework. By leveraging graph theoretic concepts and optimizing model parameters via non-conventional methods, we demonstrate significant improvements in predicting real-world data compared to standard Gaussian process methods.

The optimal detection method for urban road systems using a mobile device in vehicles is investigated, focusing on the detection of roads, lanes, and areas within a single trip and the detection of road types across multiple trips. A framework consisting of lane detection and area identification steps is presented, with a scoring system for evaluating the accuracy of road type detection. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its implementation on a large dataset of 600,000 trips and the results show that it achieves a road type detection accuracy of 83.52%. Furthermore, this approach is shown to be robust in terms of its performance with varying ride-sharing vehicle speeds and locations within cities.

Our research delves into the significance of neutrino and dark energy sector interactions using the example of an electroweak dark sector, specifically within the context of an invisible $J/\psi$ decay. To gain insights, we first examine the production of a dark energy particle and a photon within the $B$ meson, and then establish the relationship between the dark sector and semileptonic $B$ meson decays. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the dark sector and semileptonic $B$ meson decays through effective field theories, and we also explore the significance of neutrino and dark energy sector interactions using the example of an electroweak dark sector, specifically within the context of an invisible $J/\psi$ decay. To gain insights, we first examine the production of a dark energy particle and a photon within the $B$ meson, and then establish the relationship between the dark sector and semileptonic $B$ meson decays. To do this, we use the example of an invisible $J/\psi$ decay, and we demonstrate that current experimental data from the LHCb collaboration poses significant constraints on the parameters of the model, with some parameters already ruled out by current experimental data, with others approaching the sensitivity limit. Moreover, we find that future experimental data from the LHCb and Belle II will substantially improve constraint on the parameters of the model, with many parameters expected to be ruled out by future experimental data

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) for time-dependent data sets, extending the capabilities of current spectral decomposition methods. Our research adapts the traditional singular spectrum analysis (SSA) approach for single-time series and multivariate time series, developing a new method for time-dependent data sets. The proposed MFSSA framework consists of three key components: (1) dimensionality reduction through the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a data matrix whose rows represent time points and columns correlate with variable values across those time points; (2) time-dependent SVD, where SVD is reapplied at regular intervals to account for variations across time; and (3) feature selection based on the singular spatial pattern at each time point. The selected features are used to reconstruct a residual component for each time point. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MFSSA through applications to real-world datasets, including climate variability analysis and medical diagnosis using electroencephalogram data.

Deep learning-based automated driving emergency assistance systems can fall prey to cunning adversaries through malicious label manipulation, causing the system to become unstable or overly responsive. Despite being crucial for safe implementation, there is a lack of systematic analysis to understand this vulnerability. This paper examines the underlying causes of this instability in single-image architectures, specifically in relation to the self-excitation of feature maps, and identifies two key factors: the excessive amplification of minor features and the incomplete suppression of dominant features. To address this issue, the paper presents two defense frameworks for both training and inference stages. During training, a novel regression-based robust target mask framework is proposed to minimize the influence of malicious labels and reduce the gap between the classification loss and robust target mask. Conversely, defense strategies for inference stage involve modifying the activation function and introducing a feature normalization layer to mitigate the excessive amplification of minor features and prevent self-excitation. The proposed methods are evaluated on the BDD100K dataset, and the findings are examined through qualitative and quantitative analysis.

This paper examines the ultimate persistence of a one-dimensional random walk with drift, specifically focusing on its local duration with an asymptotic characteristic $\alpha$ less than one. Previously established results for $\alpha$ greater than one are contrasted to identify new circumstances for $\alpha$ between one and half, particularly when it equals three-quarters, for which there are an infinite number of solutions for the recurrence probability of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma plasma generator with a 1-meter long plasma chamber produces plasma essential for these experiments. This study focuses on optimizing the plasma generator's performance in helicon mode. Initially, the plasma is created using a combination of RF waves and gas discharges, but to improve reliability, a separate RF source is used to generate plasma in helicon mode. However, this approach has not been thoroughly validated for this configuration. To address this, the study examines plasma properties in both methods, comparing plasma density, electron temperature, and Konrad probe measurements. It finds that the most reliable method for producing plasma involves using the helicon source alone, as this produces a plasma with the same characteristics as the initial method, except for a slightly lower electron temperature. Notably, this study shows that applying 200 A of current to the helicon source produces the highest plasma density in the middle of the plasma chamber.

In this study, we develop a theoretical model that considers a pathogen-resistant host population and investigates the impact of antibiotic resistance in bacteria. The model aims to evaluate the efficacy of using bacteria as a biological control method to suppress an invasive plant species. We examine the model's equilibrium points and conduct a stability analysis to identify the conditions required for the model's solution to be free from oscillatory behavior. Additionally, we investigate the model's solution when the model's system is subject to periodic impulsive control, where the model's solution exhibits more complex behavior due to the presence of periodic disturbances.

In 2019, the MICCAI conference hosted a challenge aimed at creating an automatic system for marking and classifying individual cells within a specific region of a colorectal histology image.  This cell marking task, also known as MI-ONCO, focused on identifying and delineating nuclei within specific areas of colorectal tissue samples.  A new detection system, known as W-Net, has been developed in response to this challenge.  This detection system is unique in that it simultaneously produces both a precise mask and a more general region of interest (ROI) for each nucleus.  To train W-Net, only the ROI is annotated in the training dataset, making it more feasible to use this system for marking nuclei across multiple types of tissues.  Experiments conducted on the provided training dataset and two separate testing datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of W-Net, resulting in outstanding performance when compared to other leading detection systems according to various evaluation metrics.

We provide a characterization for extensions of odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups in a region, specifically focusing on those with a specific dimension property. This characterization offers a key insight, allowing us to prove a related conjecture originally posed by Kowalski and others. To achieve this, we employ an innovative approach, combining elements of an earlier strategy developed by Sharif and myself, along with a distinct method. Furthermore, our findings can be viewed as an extension of a previously established result from a different context.

A graph G is considered to have an iterated line graph n times, noted as G~n, if it has undergone n line graph transformations. Detectable G, denoted as d(G), is a set that contains all the hamiltonian cycles in G. This paper's objective is to examine the relationship between d(G~n) and G's hamiltonian route index, HRI(G), specifically to determine if having a higher HRI(G) value increases the likelihood of detecting more hamiltonian cycles in subsequent iterated line graphs.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to SARS-CoV-2 transmission through the disruption of cellular barriers. Pyroptosis is primarily initiated by the NLRP3 inflammasome, which can be activated as a result of mitochondrial damage caused by the virus's entry into host cells. This study develops a solitary-cell model to examine the NLRP3 inflammasome's activation and cell death due to pyroptosis, and explore how anti-inflammatory interventions affect these processes. In particular, the impact of IL-1RA, a cytokine with potential to reduce NLRP3 activation, is investigated.

External influences can significantly impact an agent's interaction with its environment. This paper seeks to remove extrinsic rewards and state parameters from reinforcement learning environments, allowing the agent to focus solely on intrinsic discoveries. A new reward system is presented, which is entirely derived from the agent's experiences within the environment. This reward scheme is utilized in a state-free framework, where the agent's understanding of the environment replaces traditional state parameters. Reinforcement learning is the underlying method used to train the agent in both systems.

A blockchain-based smart contract on the Tezos network, named HELMHOLTZ, is being developed in association with the Inria Inukshi toolset. Both projects aim to validate the correct behavior of contracts by checking initial and incoming states against specified properties. Essentially, HELMHOLTZ leverages refinement types and type inference from Inukshi's refinement type system to execute and verify contracts on the Tezos blockchain.

Deep Neural Networks, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have achieved remarkable performance in various machine learning tasks. Their widespread adoption can be attributed to their effective combination of parameter efficiency and impressive accuracy. However, the complex interlayer connections within GCNNs make it challenging to interpret their operations, particularly the convolutional processes. This study aims to provide an in-depth exploration of the matched filtering property of GCNNs, offering a comprehensive mathematical framework that facilitates a detailed analysis of the filter functions. By examining the GCNN filter bank, we derive a closed-form expression for the output of each layer, offering valuable insights into the network's behavior. These findings, in turn, inform the development of an optimization framework that addresses overfitting, an omnipresent challenge in machine learning. By applying this framework, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a series of experiments on multiple datasets, leading to a notable improvement in performance.

By modifying the Chern-Simons action with an additional scalar field, we are able to relate gravity to a gauge force within a specific framework. This modification allows for the description of both rotating, hairy black holes and solitons within this gauge framework. It also enables the exploration of solitons and black holes with non-zero temperature in a unified manner. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that a change in the Chern-Simons coefficient is equivalent to a soliton-black hole transition, depending on whether the coefficient is greater than, less than, or equal to a certain critical value.

We establish a comprehensive theory for integrating closed curves and the reverse planar graph isomorphism in the context of a single type of particle, particularly for an interacting particle system on a plane that interacts with a planar graph through a curvature-induced potential, and we show that this system maintains a non-reversible reverse symmetry. Additionally, our model includes a type of particle that interacts with the boundary of a curve through a tension-induced potential, and we prove that these models can be used to automate tasks that are challenging for humans, such as recognizing digital patterns and converting them into an analog format, and correcting imperfections in those patterns.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathology by identifying the mechanical properties of tissues. It relies on accurate estimation of tissue displacement in different directions to derive these mechanical properties. The process of synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasonic imaging has been deemed suitable for elastography; however, the method's virtual origin SA (VOSA) technique has shown better performance. The VOSA method involves the synthetic creation of virtual transducer sources equivalent to the actual physical sources. This results in more stable and precise lateral displacement estimation in comparison to the conventional SA technique. The basis of this improved estimation is the reduced grating lobe interference specific to the VOSA method. The advantages of VOSA-led elastography imaging have been experimentally validated using phantom models and human subjects. The studies indicate that the VOSA technique yields displacement estimation with a higher precision (by 2.35-fold) and a smaller percentage error (by 2.32-fold) in comparison to the conventional SA technique. This superior performance of VOSA-led elastography imaging makes it more accurate and reliable, thus having a positive impact on medical diagnosis.

Students learn programming best through writing actual code, but providing suitable code for students to read depends on the student's level of experience. Advanced students can handle complex code, but simpler examples may be too difficult for them to follow, while beginner students might struggle with either scenario. A middle-ground approach is needed for them to effectively learn from examples of working code. A new method called "rational pseudocode" is presented, aimed at helping students in the middle stage of programming education by providing a clear, readable representation of code that is similar to real programming language code. This method can be used to create examples of working code that can be understood by students in this stage, and a specific implementation of this method in the form of a language called "RationalPython" is also presented. A user-friendly interface is available to create and share RationalPython code, and several examples of this type of code are also provided. The concept of a Ramsey character for a given structure, when applied to the Boolean algebras with their natural action, yields the Ramsey degree of the Boolean algebras, a value that can be infinite. A subcollection of Boolean algebras with minimal Ramsey degree are the finitely generated, countable Boolean algebras with a V-shaped poset as their anti-chains. This paper aims to expand the list of these subcollections by defining and determining the minimal Ramsey degree of the Boolean algebras with two or three anti-chains.

In the context of large-scale datasets, a significant challenge arises when attempting to develop an efficient clustering algorithm. This issue becomes particularly pronounced in statistical learning applications, given the common practice of running multiple experiments with different random samples from the available data. To address this problem, a new dynamic k-means algorithm was developed to facilitate simultaneous clustering of all seen data points. The algorithm's performance is guaranteed by establishing an upper bound on its regret relative to an optimal solution, taking into account the total number of clustering operations and data points processed. Furthermore, experiments have demonstrated the practical advantages of this approach, particularly in high-dimensional spaces where traditional dynamic k-means methods struggle to converge. The new algorithm's effectiveness is shown across a variety of datasets and visualization scenarios.

We observe a widespread occurrence in multi-agent systems, where cooperative agents outperform their individual components, due to the lack of a universal framework that incorporates heterogeneous communication patterns. As a step to address this, we present a hierarchical framework that incorporates various structures in a collaborative pursuit-evasion game, involving multiple agents with distinct levels of communication. Our analysis provides insights into the survival probabilities of the fleeing agents, based on different hierarchical configurations, including graph topology and levels of communication. Specifically, we investigate the efficacy of connected systems, isolated groups, and hierarchical structures in achieving optimal outcomes. Our findings can be applied across a broad spectrum of multi-agent systems, involving various objective functions and game theoretic frameworks.

We examine the concept of a circular or nontransitive probability distribution, which arises when the order of certain random outcomes is unknown and may rotate or shift. Our analysis focuses on the essential requirement for a distribution to be circular or nontransitive, which involves specific symmetry coefficients. We discuss how these coefficients interact with other measures of distributional symmetry, such as circular and rectangular symmetry. We also present an example of a nontransitive probability distribution, along with the corresponding code for generating it. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between circular and nontransitive distributions and the ability to update probabilities through conditional expectations. We establish conditions under which a distribution with circular or nontransitive probabilities can be applied to multiple independent experiments. This framework is demonstrated with an example of a circular probability distribution in an exponential family.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in processing multiple types of medical images simultaneously. However, the existing cycleGAN frameworks have primarily focused on natural image transformations, with limited work applying them to medical imaging. Furthermore, most current medical image processing applications use supervised learning techniques, utilizing paired training data to fuse low-dose CT images with their paired high-dose CT images. In contrast, the unsupervised cycleGAN method leverages paired data from both low-dose and high-dose CT images in an unsupervised learning process. Although this approach has been successful in transforming natural images, it is unknown how effective it would be for processing low-dose CT images. In this paper, we explore the application of the unsupervised cycleGAN framework in enhancing low-dose CT images. To improve the cycleGAN algorithm, we modified it to include an adaptive inception layer that allows for two-dimensional data transformations, with the goal of minimizing the reconstruction error while maintaining the image's entropy. To prevent the overfitting of heavy CT images, we added a batch normalization layer to the unsupervised cycleGAN module. With the proposed method, we achieved a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 11.16%, a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 37.67

Continuing issues with massive amounts of unlabeled data hindering dialogue comprehension tasks highlight the value of semi-supervised learning methods.  To leverage both labeled and unlabeled dialogue data, we present a novel semi-supervised pre-training approach called SPACE-2, which utilizes contrastive learning on self-organized tree structures to unite two types of data.  Through contrastive loss functions, SPACE-2 reduces the gap between two types of data by incorporating unlabeled dialogue contexts as fake labeled data.  To refine the structure of the tree, we propose a novel tree-merging algorithm, and to model dialogue comprehensions, we suggest a minimalistic tree encoder that combines token-level and node-level representations.  Experimental evaluations on diverse dialogue comprehension tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of SPACE-2, and by scaling up the model to large datasets, we discover that semi-supervised learning outperforms fully supervised methods.  Achieving state-of-the-art performance on DIALOG-State Verification and Relational Question Answering tasks, SPACE-2 also exhibits superior performance on human-human conversation verification.  However, on Role Recognition and Multi-step Dialogue State Tracking tasks, SPACE-2 underperforms with smaller datasets, but with larger datasets, it matches or surpasses competition performance.

This research focuses on an ideal fluid spacetime with conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton, and we determine the metric configuration under certain conditions applied to an open and closed manifold. Specifically, if the manifold is open, we find that a certain equation is equivalent to another equation when a specific vector is zero. When the manifold is closed, we establish relationships between several functions derived from the given equations, and we also find the geometric configuration when the soliton is in equilibrium.

To study the distortions and rotations of semi-magic nuclei, we employed the angular momentum projection method onto spheroidal shapes. Our self-consistent calculations used the finite-range liquid drop model for the distortion and rotation energies and the deformed single-particle potential. We examined the spin distribution within the ground and excited states of halos such as $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg, and $^{16}$O to understand how shape uncoupling affects rotational patterns.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade the BasicVSR framework by incorporating an advanced propagation pathway and using a deformable alignment mechanism, which enables the efficient utilization of temporal patterns across multiple hours in video. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits a seamless integration with existing video restoration tasks, and through comprehensive experimentation, we demonstrate its robust performance on video super-resolution and three other tasks - video deinterlacing, frame rate upscaling, and video to image super-resolution.

This study proposes an efficient new method to estimate jet energy using the collision data collected at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically for muon collisions at an energy level of 13 TeV. The approach, which utilizes the collision events involving two muons, enables precise energy measurements for antiprotons, protons, and heavy ions. The new method surpasses the existing jet energy correction factors, providing an alternative means of jet energy calibration. Building on previous research, our model develops a new function to represent the distribution of electron energy, which is derived from primary electrons resulting from heavy flavor hadron decays. The solution to the vector boson estimation problem involves employing two functions to model the energy spectra of electrons and muons. The model for muon energy spectrum relies on 11 parameters, whereas the model for electron energy spectrum, which is more complex, is represented by 22 parameters. The proposed estimation method is compared to the current LHC calibration, and our results demonstrate a level of accuracy at least as precise as existing standards, with some cases reaching an improvement of 10%.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, models are often shared across tasks to capitalize on their common elements of structure. Yet, when a task is significantly different from the others, using a shared model can actually impede learning by introducing negative performance due to model predictions that are the result of destructive interference. This concept is particularly evident in scenarios where the tasks share a common underlying structure but have distinct functional forms. Our research reveals that when a shared model is used in such situations, the value function represents a superposition of multiple systems that are linked but distinct. We then develop a technique for learning multi-task systems that are linked but distinct, and verify our approach through simulations in both model-based multi-task reinforcement learning and the extension to model-free methods. Our results show that our method achieves better performance when compared to standard multi-task reinforcement learning algorithms in scenarios where the tasks share a common underlying structure but have distinct functional forms.

This paper deals with two types of PDEs - specifically the porous medium type and the rapid diffusion type - within a broad, non-compact metric measure space with a compact boundary. We establish various estimates for the approximation of their gradients using different methods, mainly based on the BMO boundedness of their operators. This, in turn, enables us to derive key results including the boundedness of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation, the continuity of the nonlinear operator, and ultimately the convergence of a specific iterative process.

Kurt Godel, along with Alfred Tarski, Hans Hahn, and Joseph Schachte, discussed various logical concepts in 1931. From this meeting, Tarski developed an idea for formulating the concept of truth models, which he later implemented in a 1933 paper with Arthur Burks. In 1935, Godel, together with Tarski, Robert Solovay, and others, explored the consistency of various axioms, including those proposed by Tarski in his 1933 paper. Furthermore, Godel, Tarski, and Emil Post participated in the Princeton Bicentennial Conference on Mathematics in 1936, where discussion on the consistency of the axiom of choice took place. This paper delves into the history of Godel's work on the incompleteness theorems and the development of model theory.

This paper formulates three-sphere theorems for functions solving a specific type of linear differential equation, drawing on techniques from algebra and geometry. Specifically, we establish three-sphere theorems for functions in $\mathbb{R}^n$ related to the Dirac operator, utilizing a formula that expresses this operator in terms of the Clifford product. We then demonstrate how this approach yields results analogous to those derived in [RSS], [RT], and [RS] for functions satisfying certain differential equations in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$. We also introduce a factorization method capable of treating the higher-dimensional case $\mathbb{R}^4$.

When conducting surveys on a geographic basis, a balanced design is crucial to ensure that data is collected from diverse areas in proportion to specified criteria. The process of human identification and recruitment for such studies can be lengthy and time-consuming due to the need to adhere to strict balance constraints. A method called sequential geographically balanced sampling has been developed as a solution to tackle these challenges. This method allows for the recruitment of new subjects in sequence while maintaining balance constraints at both the national and local levels. As a result, it enables the efficient inclusion of a steady flow of new participants in research in which geographic balance is crucial.

To facilitate flexible robotic grasping and manipulation, an eye-in-hand camera is essential for providing real-time visual feedback. However, adjusting the camera's position and orientation to acquire optimal images is a challenging problem that has not been extensively researched. Based on our study, we developed a novel approach to resolve this issue by utilizing a single image to determine the camera settings for maximum information gain. Our method first analyzes the image's features and assesses their importance in defining the camera's optimal position and orientation. To prevent overfitting, we implemented a random sampling strategy to ensure a diverse range of models is trained on natural data. Our experiments demonstrated that our proposed method can effectively find camera settings that yield high-quality images and outperforms a baseline method in both evaluation metrics and task efficiency.

In scenarios like missing data recovery, inverse problems, and semi-supervised learning, generating a target posterior distribution is crucial. In such cases, traditional methods like MCMC face significant challenges when the target distribution is complex or the missing data is substantial. Current machine learning techniques, including GANs, excel at modeling high-dimensional probability distributions, but often produce low-quality samples when trained to focus on both density and discriminative aspects. A new approach was required to overcome these limitations. We propose a innovative technique for conditioning on partial input data, along with a framework that integrates regularization to recover the posterior distribution. The method leverages two main components: a conditionally trained discriminator with auxiliary information, and a quantitative metric to enforce agreement with the target data. The framework is further enhanced by incorporating parallel neural networks to achieve model regularization and reduce overfitting. The proposed approach was evaluated on synthetic data, missing data recovery, and semi-supervised classification, and the experiments demonstrated its superiority over existing methods.

This article examines the concept of locally invariant surfaces in dynamical systems of a specific order and extends this inquiry to non-local surfaces in fractional-order dynamical systems. We establish a key theoretical framework stating that in a dynamical system of order $\alpha$, a non-local surface cannot be an invariant surface unless it is entirely comprised of equilibrium points. This overarching principle is then applied to a particular fractional-order system with a specific type of surface of attraction, leading to an observable result in the field of economics.

Next-generation wireless networks requiring ultra-high data rates can be supported by Terahertz communications, which involve direct long-distance transmissions and multi-hop cooperative transmissions between users and base stations. This research focuses on optimizing a crucial step in these communications processes called beam training, which involves identifying the optimal wireless links and corresponding directions for data transmission. Initially, a process called deep learning-based beam training is introduced, which employs a neural network to recognize the best links and determine associated training directions through repeated experiments, with the goal of maximizing long-term data transmission rates. To improve efficiency, a new approach called reinforcement learning-based beam training is proposed, which allows the learning process to focus on critical links and reduce unnecessary training. Analytical and simulated results show that both deep learning-based and reinforcement learning-based beam training outperform traditional methods, with the latter offering enhanced performance efficiency.

The line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16 contains a Scintillation Bubble with unusual properties, allowing us to study the interstellar medium in the Galactic plane with a high level of detail. By analyzing signal variations as the Earth and pulsar rotate, our research reveals a previously undetected structure within the bubble lasting from around 1940 UT on 2019-01-02 to 0340 UT on 2019-01-03. This duration is significantly longer than expected, at around 72 hours, and we believe it may be caused by a massive overdensity on the solar side, with a density ratio of approximately 1.5. By examining how matter moves through this overdensity as the Earth and pulsar change positions, we gain valuable insights into the long-axis length of the structure, estimating it to be around 0.25 parsecs. By sharing our radiowave data and analysis tools, we aim to advance scintillation research and invite fellow scientists to build upon our findings.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic dilated convolution filter widths. Secondly, a cascaded network architecture is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in an efficient manner. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of this model in producing more realistic audio at unsupported frequencies and shorter synthesis lengths with similar quality, compared to the baseline WaveNet.

This research presents a novel web-based platform called MADARi, which offers a user-friendly interface for annotating Arabic texts morphologically and systematically corrects the spelling in real-time. By leveraging machine learning algorithms, MADARi enhances the quality of annotations made by human annotators and tackles the challenges posed by varying Arabic scripts, including Common Descriptive Rich Eschars and Literal Descriptive Rich Eschars, that have not been extensively addressed in previous annotation tools. Additionally, MADARi addresses spelling errors during the annotation process, ensuring that annotated texts are both semantically rich and linguistically accurate.

As exoplanets are increasingly found in temperate orbits, understanding how they interact with their stellar environment and biological indicators becomes increasingly vital. This process is complicated by the presence of gas in these planets' atmospheres, which affects their spectral patterns. In a recent study, the spectrum of a temperate exoplanet in the Hubble Space Telescope's wavelength range was analyzed for various species of gases, including metals and molecules that are essential for life. To achieve this, the team of researchers used the SPICE radiative transfer code, combining their results to synthesize the exoplanet's visible and near-infrared spectrum. By applying this analysis to the planet known as Kepler-167 e, the scientists discovered that its atmosphere could contain high levels of gas, consisting of various elements, gases that indicate biological activity, and gases that form due to the planet's interaction with its star. However, more precise techniques, such as the use of transit spectra and light curves, are needed to accurately analyze these atmospheres. In addition, studying these atmospheres, as shown with the case of Kepler-167 e, can provide valuable insights into the planet's physical properties and its environment.

To identify Majorana modes through tunneling spectroscopy, we must distinguish the signature of a Majorana peak, which follows a V-shape, from the similar-looking peaks of other quasiparticles. The presence of an ohmic gap in the tunneling conductance at low voltage poses a challenge. To overcome this, we suggest using a different electrode material with a higher resistance, increasing the tunneling resistance to the point where an ohmic gap becomes evident in the tunneling conductance at higher voltages. This method may provide a more reliable way to distinguish the Majorana peak, based on the conductance's energy dependence.

The development of an advanced road defect detection and asset management system, called RoadAtlas, is presented in this paper. This innovative solution utilizes artificial intelligence, enabling the automatic identification of road flaws and characteristics from image data, and providing real-time feedback for efficient data collection and vehicle routing. Building on existing research, RoadAtlas offers a comprehensive and versatile platform, capable of analyzing various image types and detecting a broad range of road defects and features. Additionally, the system offers multiple data collection strategies and vehicle routing options designed to minimize costs and improve quality of service.

Comparative evaluations between model-based and model-free methods can provide valuable insights into localization performance. Our study supplements existing research on model-free head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) by conducting an in-depth analysis of model-based binaural synthesis techniques. We investigated three approaches to sound synthesis, ranging from basic pulse-based methods to complex geometric models, to examine their ability to replicate natural sound perception. Although these techniques can accurately recreate certain acoustic properties, they struggle with other fundamental aspects of sound perception, such as distance and velocity. Our findings suggest that these issues arise because these models overlook certain key psychological components, including the internal coordinate system and the auditory scene complexity. We further observed that these model-based techniques can produce unrealistic auditory experiences, such as visualizing sound sources inside the head or misinterpreting the sound's envelope. In contrast, our previous research established that HRTF-based synthesis produces locally accurate sound perception but falls short in other dimensions. These findings have significant implications for the development of more comprehensive sound synthesis methods, particularly in environments beyond the immediate surroundings.

Current graph neural networks are designed to operate within the Euclidean framework, but our proposal extends this scope to the Lorentzian metric. By doing so, we incorporate directionality and invariance to transformation, leading to enhanced neural network performance. Specifically, our model exhibits sensitivity to graph directionality and invariance to global and local transformations, including orthogonal transformations, translations, and node permutations. Moreover, it achieves state-of-the-art validation accuracy on six extensive real-world classification datasets spanning correlation and citation networks.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source domain within a structural acoustic model. The source domain in question is a vibrating structure located behind a acoustic wall, and it generates sound waves in a confined acoustic space. The objective is to recover the vibrating structure, given measurements of the resulting sound waves, and we achieve this using a combination of the finite element method and a nonconforming mesh setup. Our approach involves two major components: first, the sound waves are modeled using the weak form, and this is solved using a nonconforming mesh technique; second, the vibrating structure is modeled using the strong form, and this is solved using a conforming mesh technique. This dual mesh setup allows us to apply boundary conditions in a manner consistent with the original problem, and thus obtain an accurate representation of the source domain. This research is centered around a specific model consisting of a cylindrical acoustic space and a source domain in the form of a circular disk. However, the developed algorithm is capable of handling more complex models consisting of various shapes.

A new method has been developed for optomechanical compression, which involves coupling a optical cavity linked to a laser system to a mechanical object within that cavity. The interaction between these components generates a complex phenomenon where a high-energy photon is split into two smaller energy photons. This process is maintained in a stable state through a continuous feedback loop. A key feature of this method is the ability to precisely control the operation either through a simple, direct approach or by utilizing a complex reservoir of light. A critical parameter in optomechanical compression is the distinction between two possible states, which includes either the hybrid optomechanical model itself or an alternative model in which the optomechanical interaction is replaced by another type of phenomenon. Steady-state compression transfer can occur in both models, but they behave differently in certain situations.

We enhance the basic $\mu$-calculus with modal mu to include various modal mu calculi particles such as symmetry, co-arithmeticity, and fixed-point operators, either globally or within specific scopes. Our formulation is developed for both the scalar and vectorial mu calculi. We demonstrate the efficacy of these extensions through their ability to encode key modal mu calculi fragments, including the symmetric and propositional projective modal mu calculi. Moreover, we present both deterministic and non-deterministic decision procedures for the scalar and vectorial mu-calculi with the symmetry operator.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model, incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Bieleck and Kula (2019). We derive an intuitive formal
justification for this model and demonstrate its potential to capture impulsive
behaviors exhibited in tasks involving limited data points. Additionally, we
investigate the model's implications for the hyperbolic and exponential delay
discounting models.

We have examined Harmonic Gauge Theory in both $F(R)$ gravity and $f(R,~\Box)~\phi^4$ field theory as examples of non-linear gauge theories.  By applying a linearized variation principle, we derived the gauge equations and their associated propagators for both theories, taking into consideration the effects of quantum fluctuations represented by the box operator.  Our findings indicate that both theories have no problematic divergences when using the Harmonic Gauge.  Furthermore, we found that in $f(R,~\Box)$ gravity, the Higgs type mechanism can be employed to resolve the naturalness issue that arises when the Higgs field is zero, as occurs in standard $R$-gravity.  In addition, we found that in $F(R)$ gravity, the Higgs field can be used to resolve the naturalness issue, but this requires it to have a non-zero value even when the scalar curvature vanishes.  Our investigation also reveals that both theories exhibit an asymptotically free behavior at very high energies, but this may be viewed as an undesirable feature.  Finally, we found that in $f(R,~\Box)~\phi^4$ field theory, the Higgs type mechanism cannot resolve the naturalness issue, but this is addressed by introducing an additional polynomial term in the Ricci tensor, which then becomes infinitely large at very high energies and thus limits the theory's applicability to energies below the Planck scale.

A positive definite matrix is an extension of a symmetric matrix by a vector, representing a quadratic form that can be re-expressed as a sum of squared distances. Given two matrices A and B, if there's a homomorphism from the signed graph associated with A to the signed graph associated with B, then B contains an extension of A. This relationship between matrix combinations and graph homomorphisms is explored in relation to the concept of extended double covers in a paper that also discusses a specific application involving the limits of homomorphism numbers for certain types of graphs.

In the context of quantum thermodynamics, a method is presented for transforming canonical density matrices into Weyl-Wigner representations. This transformation enables the visualization of the quantum fluctuations of physical properties in real-phase-space. Consequently, we derive the condition for thermal equilibrium in an isolated quantum system using Weyl-Wigner representations. Additionally, we apply this approach to demonstrate that, in thermal equilibrium, the mean values of position and momentum in the Weyl-Wigner representation satisfy the classical equation of motion. A further application involves examining the fluctuations of an observable in an isolated quantum system at thermal equilibrium.

I would like to offer a few optimistic thoughts regarding the concept of negative absolute temperature, which has been widely discussed and debated among physicists. Over the years, a clear distinction has emerged between two main groups: those who consider negative temperature a mere theoretical abstraction, and those who have successfully incorporated it into their practical understanding. As we reflect on the progress made so far, it's evident that the latter group's approach has been more productive in the end. While negative temperature may seem intricate and complex, we believe that the key to a deeper understanding lies in viewing it as a unified framework, encompassing both theoretical and applied aspects. This talk is a collection of my own notes and thoughts on this topic, which I hope will spark further discussion and debate.

We explore a well-known concept in number theory known as sumsets, specifically focusing on constrained sumsets where integers can be assigned either positive or negative values. Our research investigates the basic principle that for any given integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$, the set $a_1x_1 + a_2x_2 + \ldots + a_nx_n = 0$ contains at least $2^n$ solutions $(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)$. Our work also considers the converse outcome and its implications.

Characterizing the molecular features of colorectal polyps is crucial to develop accurate classification methods detecting malignancy and assessing dysplasia, which are critical for effective early treatment and follow-up. Recent studies utilizing deep learning techniques have achieved notable classification performance. However, training these models requires vast amounts of annotated histological images, which are typically scarce due to the time-consuming and specialized process of tissue analysis. In this study, we introduce UniToPatho, a substantial dataset comprising 8626 regions of interest (ROI) extracted from 871 full-field images of colorectal polyps, which have been labeled by expert pathologists as normal, adenomatous, carcinomatous, or hyperplastic. UniToPatho also includes 318 images divided into four categories for training and evaluating deep learning-based classification models. To demonstrate the utility of UniToPatho, we established a simple yet robust model comprising two consecutive layers, which achieved exceptional performance on the test dataset. Notably, our findings surpass the current state-of-the-art performance reported for the classification of colorectal polyps.

A novel numerical method has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems, particularly those involving smooth variations in material properties. This method can handle objects with smooth surfaces and is an alternative to traditional approaches based on short wave asymptotics. It relies on a scaled boundary element formulation with a scaled operator approach, is highly versatile, and can be implemented using flexible finite element techniques. However, a significant drawback of this method is the computationally intensive requirement to store a substantial number of matrices associated with the scaled operator. Until now, there was no established way to execute this method using an in-memory storage model. We have developed a new, streamlined implementation that utilizes a factorized sparse storage approach, reducing memory requirements and making it feasible to solve these complex problems on a typical desktop computer. This has enabled us to achieve significant gains in computational efficiency, and our results demonstrate exceptional convergence when compared to the traditional hybrid approach.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in two distinct chondrite meteorites: Chelyabinsk and Benenitra. Our research indicates these meteorites have similar hydrogen isotopic signatures that differ from existing estimates of solar nebula and planchette chondrites, specifically Planchette chondrite-like objects in the inner solar system such as Tenerrife and Saint-Aubin. Furthermore, we found Benenitra and Chelyabinsk have similar water content, suggesting it's a critical parameter for assigning meteorites to specific planetary sources. Based on their isotopic composition, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk can be linked to accretion of dry inner solar system planetesimals, followed by a moisture-rich delivery from short-period comets during the late stages of planetary formation in the inner solar system.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for key quantities including ground-state expectations, correlation functions, and form factors for higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin value and number of sites. Additionally, we demonstrate that the symmetry of the infinite system is represented by an affine quantum algebra, specifically $A_{2r-1}^{(1)}$, under specific conditions for certain higher-spin XXZ chains. This phenomenon occurs for both odd and even numbers of spins.

Language barriers pose a significant challenge in global communication, and an individual's ability to express thoughts in a different language is crucial. Currently available translation solutions primarily focus on written text, leaving a void in voice-based translations. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel concept of zero-shot voice translation, which enables individuals to convey a message in one language and hear the equivalent message in another language. Building upon state-of-the-art models for zero-shot cross-lingual speech translation, we present a simplified framework that directly pairs speech with targeted languages. Our model's basic architecture leverages a shared neural module for both encoding audio inputs and decoding text outputs, allowing for translation without pre-trained parallel corpora. Notably, our study demonstrates the efficacy of this model in translating speech between multiple languages without prior training on parallel datasets, thereby offering a pioneering solution for zero-shot voice translation.

We introduce local multilayered linearizations for conducting and optic materials that go beyond the long wavelength approximation. This method can be applied to a wide range of frequencies, spanning both acoustic and optical fields within complex geometries. We then develop a multilayered linearization for groups of materials that are linked by smooth boundaries, and demonstrate its connection to the Mie theory. Building on this foundation, we create a multilocal linearization for disparate materials with sharp interfaces, and prove its equivalence to a combination of Mie theory and effective medium theory. This approach can be used to calculate scattering, field distribution, and energy flux within these systems. We demonstrate the success of this method with numerical experiments, achieving highly accurate results even when the original approximation methods fail.

This study introduces three key concepts: quantum immanents, double Young-Capelli bitableaux and Schur altered symmetric functions, which are interconnected and provide the framework for an upcoming, more comprehensive exploration. 

The position of a double Young-Celli bitableau within a given Schur altered symmetric function class can be determined using a specific combinatorial approach, derived from the principles underlying the quantum immanents property. 

By leveraging the Capelli and Schur altered symmetric function specialists, the interconnections between the involved combinatorial objects can be understood from a representation theory perspective, revealing connections to the irreducible representations of the U(n) unitary group. 

A specific algebraic algorithm, utilizing the quantum and classical divided difference operators, can be employed to change the support of a given Schur altered symmetric function, effectively achieving this by applying the BGG (Bose-Einstein statistics) correspondence. 

A particular instance of this algebraic process results in the derivation of an explicit formula for the eigenfunctions of an associated differential operator, which can be recognized as the Hamiltonian operator from soliton theory, specifically in the Phases I and II cases. 

By transforming the BGG correspondence, we can also obtain the underlying combinatorial data for an arbitrary intertableaux, given an initial standard tableaux within a specific Schur altered symmetric function class, by applying the quantum immanents property in an inverse manner.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the implications of combining it with minimal dark matter. By incorporating a minimal dark matter sector consisting of one WIMP field, we derive the effective potential for the Higgs field and establish the stability conditions for the Higgs vacuum. Additionally, we determine the direct and indirect detection channels for dark matter within this combined theory, and utilize the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO package to derive the relevant cross-sections and recoil spectra. Furthermore, we define the parameter space based on the likelihood puzzle, reindeer bounds, and metastability conditions, and present the resulting pheno-regions through probability maps. These regions, where the model's parameters conform to theoretical and experimental constraints, provide the possible ranges for the scalar sector parameters within this combined theory.

We employ a spin-orbit coupled $d$-only model to examine the electronic structure of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal oxides, focusing on how the band structure and spectral function change as the band width varies. Especially in the lower band width limit, strong correlations cause the intense splitting of the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbitals. However, as the band width increases towards a more atomic-like behavior, the splitting between these orbitals decreases, with the $e_g$ states moving downwards in energy. Notably, in lower band width compounds, the Efros-Shklovskii hole, resulting from $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, presents itself as a $e_g$ like state. Furthermore, our theoretical framework is applicable to understanding experimental results, specifically spectroscopic data, and offers insight into the unique properties exhibited by these compounds through close comparison with available experimental evidence.

This research examines how relative quantum representations of a braid from a 3-manifold, sharing a boundary with a linked collection of tubular neighborhoods, changes under a type of topological transformation called a birational alteration. We successfully demonstrate that this representation's behavior is consistent and predictable across various such alterations, ensuring that it retains key properties. Furthermore, we show that the representation's behavior can be understood through the principles of a specific geometric framework, known as degenerate mixed characteristic version, although this connection is previously established only for a limited subset of transformations.

The accuracy of machine learning models, in particular those using radiography for diagnosis, can be impacted by external visual factors such as lighting, camera angle and quality of images. This distortion can hinder the performance of these models. Image preprocessing techniques are already employed to enhance the quality of images. However, developing algorithms that take into account the specific characteristics of radiographs and adapt to variations in image quality due to the underlying illness is an area that needs further research. In this paper, we examine the effects of pulmonary nodules on chest X-rays and investigate new techniques for enhancing image quality. Our experiments reveal that a combination of techniques such as contrast and brightness adjustment, together with top-cutoff filtering, yields better results than conventional techniques. Furthermore, we establish that there is no significant disparity between the performance of models trained on images modified by nodules and those trained on images modified by other illnesses.

ViDaExpert is an intuitive tool for a detailed examination of multidimensional vector data, specifically designed for an in-depth visual analysis of complex high-dimensional datasets. It enables a thorough review of vector similarities, gradient patterns, and multi-dimensional structures by offering a comprehensive, customizable interface for a thorough understanding of data landscapes. With a user-friendly approach, ViDaExpert allows for the simultaneous analysis of multiple datasets, comparative studies between datasets, and a dive into the inner workings and underlying patterns of data, making it an ideal platform for scientific research, dataset validation, and quality control.

This research involves accurately estimating gravitational forces within a two-dimensional flat region, using Isaac Newton's formulation, by breaking the area into smaller parts and combining the force measurements with a precise total. A method is presented to provide a swift comparison to the exact force calculation, along with a reliable bound on the error. The challenge of determining Newton's force also sparks further inquiry into its implications in deciding boundary collisions in fluid dynamics. A new technique is proposed to predict collision times, based on an overestimation of the fluid flow field, and this method is applied to a specific problem involving a fluid flow bounded by two circular walls.
